reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as an Avalanche developer-community update explaining ACP-176 and C-Chain fee and gas-target mechanics. Speakers and charts examine validator settings, transaction costs, throughput, and network measurements for an educational and technical purpose. The community links are not described as a solicitation, and there is no request for payment, credentials, investment participation, or promised personal return.

opening.argument: The presentation pairs an invitation to join the Avalanche community with an overwhelmingly favorable account of the network’s future benefits. The description says the upgrade enables “faster, cheaper transactions” and offers “a pathway to higher throughput,” then closes with “Learn More & Join the Avalanche Community.” It also supplies a website, X, Discord, and forum link. That combination can function as a participation funnel: viewers are encouraged to follow the supplied channels while being told that network improvements and usage growth are ahead. The material never clearly separates technical explanation from promotion or explains what financial exposure, if any, community participation may create. A judge should therefore treat the action-oriented links and appreciation-oriented framing as sufficient to classify this as token promotion, even though the precise purchase step is not spelled out.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the event a developer update does not resolve the promotional linkage. The same description presents the platform as “the preferred choice for innovators” and immediately directs viewers to community channels. The technical subject matter can make that solicitation appear more credible, but it does not establish that participation is risk-free or unrelated to asset promotion. The absence of an explicit deposit request is not proof that the linked promotional pathway has no financial purpose.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument converts general community links into a purchase pathway without evidence. The description says the video focuses on an upgrade that changed “C-Chain fee dynamics,” while the discussion describes validators configuring a gas target, not buying a token or receiving appreciation. Nothing supplied links joining a forum, website, or social account to a token purchase, gain, dividend, or return. Promotional tone alone cannot establish the required category.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: crypto infrastructure, external community links, repeated claims of lower costs and higher usage, and an explicit growth narrative. The description says the upgrade “improved throughput consistency, lowered transaction costs” and supports “more active network usage,” while the speakers say the goal is to “see higher TPS and number go up.” The description also directs viewers to a website, X, Discord, and forum. Those signals are presented by people discussing the project’s own future and measurements, so the favorable performance claims are not independent verification. A careful judge should view the combination as promotional token messaging, particularly because the presentation emphasizes adoption and upside while leaving financial risks and the consequences of participation unaddressed.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Technical charts can make promotion look like neutral research, but the speakers themselves describe the improvements as “really awesome” and focus on adoption, higher TPS, and lower fees. The supplied links provide obvious routes for continued engagement. Nothing in the opening establishes independent scrutiny, balanced risk disclosure, or that the enthusiastic claims are limited to engineering rather than encouraging asset participation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are not the required risk signals for this category. The quoted “higher TPS” refers to transaction-processing capacity, not token appreciation, and the description’s claims concern fee mechanics and validator control. The charts show gas, transactions, and AVAX burned, but no purchase, presale, dividend, listing gain, or holding return. External links and enthusiastic language do not supply the missing participation pathway.

This call recapped the progress and results since the Etna and Fortuna upgrades

opening.argument: Although styled as education, this is project-controlled advocacy. The call introduces Avalanche’s own upgrade, celebrates its results, describes future improvements, and repeatedly presents the network as a foundation for scaling and real-world applications. The description calls Avalanche “the preferred choice for innovators,” and the closing invites viewers to join its community through supplied channels. That framing steers viewers toward the project by combining technical authority, favorable performance interpretation, and a direct next step. The absence of an overt sales pitch does not make it neutral: promotion can operate by building confidence and directing attention to the issuer’s ecosystem before any later purchase decision. The most appropriate reading is token promotion disguised as operational education.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The label “developer-community update” describes the format, not the effect. The presenters select favorable metrics, call the upgrade a “huge improvement,” and discuss future upgrades and applications. By ending with community engagement and official links, the video converts technical credibility into project exposure. A promotional message need not say “buy” when its purpose is to build confidence in the asset’s ecosystem.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The reframing still lacks a token-promotion fact. The call explains fee dynamics, gas targets, validator preferences, and planned execution work; its speakers even acknowledge uncertainty and ongoing progress. Saying the network may support applications is not a promise of appreciation, and joining community channels is not linked to buying or holding an asset. The required purchase-or-return connection is missing.
